content: Give me all 3 posts for this week I wanna review them

Here are all three, in one place. Post 2 is the replacement — the water version is withdrawn.

---

### Post 1 — Tuesday, AI + cyber security — 611 chars

An AI lab put its most capable vulnerability-discovery model inside the organisations that run power grids, water supplies and hospitals.

The model has flagged over 23,000 potential vulnerabilities across 1,000 open-source projects. More than 6,000 were rated high or critical.

Here is what sticks with me. The bottleneck is no longer finding bugs. It is fixing them. Human teams cannot triage and patch what an AI can find in weeks.

Discovery is solved. Remediation is not.

What happens when defenders can see every flaw but cannot fix them fast enough?

#CyberSecurity #ArtificialIntelligence #AI #InfoSec

Source: https://complexdiscovery.com/glasswing-widens-anthropic-puts-mythos-inside-power-water-and-hospital-operators-across-more-than-15-countries/

⚠️ Honest flag: this is a June 2026 development, not this week's news. It is the most concrete non-duplicative AI + cyber story I could verify against a full source. Distinct from last week's agent-autonomy theme.

---

### Post 2 — Wednesday, AI + non-cyber (employment law) — 991 chars

An AI system can flag a worker for dismissal. From next July it cannot make that dismissal stick on its own.

On 30 September a governor signed a set of workplace AI measures. One of them, the No Robo Bosses Act, says an employer may not rely solely on an automated decision system for discipline or termination. A human must corroborate the recommendation with other evidence. It takes effect on 1 July 2027.

The package goes further. Layoffs driven by AI have to be documented and disclosed. Workplace surveillance tools may not infer an employee's emotional state. Clinical AI has to ship with bias-risk checks.

What strikes me is the order. The tool arrived first, at scale, and the rule is only now catching up. The law assumes the system is already in the room.

If you are entering the workforce, this matters: the thing that screens or recommends you increasingly has to be checked by a person.

Does a human reviewing an AI recommendation change the outcome, or just the paperwork?

Sources: https://www.ebglaw.com/insights/publications/four-new-california-laws-reshape-the-rules-for-workplace-ai · https://www.sheppard.com/insights/blogs/california-signs-landmark-new-ai-workplace-laws-on-termination-layoffs-and-surveillance

Jurisdiction deliberately left unnamed under your no-countries/towns rule. Say the word if you want it named.

---

### Post 3 — Thursday, personal — 576 chars

I check suspicious emails most days. Sender address, link domain, the tone of the request.

The ones that get me are rarely the obvious ones. They are the ones where the domain is off by one character, or the display name is right but the address underneath is wrong.

I have built small tools to help with this. But the tool I trust most is still the pause. The moment of actually reading the address instead of the display name.

That pause is the whole defence.

When did you last stop and read a sender's actual email address?

#Phishing #CyberSecurity #InfoSec #Awareness

Source: your LinkedIn profile. Deliberate contrast with last week — that was about trusting systems to run unattended, this is about the human skill of noticing.
